newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan spar on trade ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan spar on trade ahead of summit.

text.p: The United States and Japan sparred with each other over the Asian nation's mounting trade surplus in what could prove to be a harbinger of tougher battles down the road.

In a meeting with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Thursday, President Bill Clinton voiced concern about the rising surplus and warned that a continued climb could spell troubles for ties between the two nations, U.S. officials said.

"The president said previous persistent trade imbalances with Japan had been a source of real damage in the bilateral relationship and it was very important ... we don't return to that type of atmosphere," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.

A senior Japanese official said that Clinton presented Hashimoto with a paper forecasting a steady climb in Japan's trade surplus in the coming months. It was not clear how long of a period the forecast covered, but the official indicated to Reuters that it was at least until the end of this year.
Hashimoto responded with a paper of his own arguing that the surplus was not likely to rise substantially in the medium term, Japanese officials said.
Japan's global trade surplus in May soared by more than 200 percent from a year earlier. Its bilateral surplus with the United States climbed by more than 90 percent.

While the United States is not pleased with the current level of the surplus -- Clinton told reporters on Thursday he wished it was not so high -- Washington seems more concerned about what lies ahead.
"Some recent indications are that there may be large trade surpluses on the not too distant horizon," Clinton economic adviser Daniel Tarullo said.
Tarullo told reporters that Clinton and Hashimoto -- who met here on the eve of the annual summit of industrial democracies -- did not discuss foreign exchange rates.

However, U.S. officials recognise that the dollar's recent drop against the yen -- it has fallen some 15 yen in the last two months -- should help contain the rise in Japan's surplus in the long-term.

A senior Japanese official, who declined to be identified, called the rise in Japan's surplus a "cyclical" response to the past weakness of the yen. Over the last two years, the yen has fallen some 45 percent against the dollar, even after taking its recent rebound into account.
"You shouldn't worry too much about cyclical factors," he told Reuters. "In a year, both Japan and the United States will be able to discuss more seriously Japan's surplus," he added.

He said that Japan cannot control the level of the exchange rate or the strength of U.S. demand for Japanese exports. What it can do is to concentrate on changing the structure of its economy so that it relies less on exports and more on domestic demand.
The official argued that such structural change is already underway, pointing, among other things, to Japan's increased propensity to import manufactured goods.
U.S. officials acknowledge that change is taking place but question whether it is as far-reaching as their Japanese counterparts maintain.
U.S. officials also seem to have their doubts about Hashimoto's willingness and ability to follow through on his promise of massive deregulation of the Japanese economy.

The two countries on Thursday agreed to set up a formal consultative process to discuss Hashimoto's deregulation efforts in specific areas. "We're here to call his bluff," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said.
